title: Six Talking Points As Liverpool and Arsenal Deliver Game of the Season So Far
subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Grey Whitebloom2:39 PM ESTArsenal edged a match of fine margins. / David Price/Arsenal FC/Getty Images“Today has to be the day,” Mikel Arteta offered up prematch, his voice strangled by a mixture of hope as much as expectation.

It had been 14 years of fruitless visits to Anfield for Arsenal, as their manager was constantly reminded. The former Everton midfielder had endured so much heartache at the home of Liverpool it had become something of a mental block. Even when the Gunners scaled the peak of the Premier League title last season, they still lost at Anfield.

That 1–0 reverse last year was a horribly tense and tight affair between two teams more afraid of losing than ambitious enough to win. Andoni Iraola’s arrival at Liverpool over the summer has blasted that attitude out of Merseyside, and the hosts dragged a reluctant Arsenal into their orbit of chaos this weekend.
Sunday proved to be the day for Arteta and his players, who desperately held on to a 1–0 win of their own which offered positives for both teams and a riotous sense of fun for the neutral.

Ezri Konsa and Gabriel were busy. / Darren Staples/AFP/Getty Images“The way that modern football is, is the way that Bournemouth play,” the most successful Premier League manager of the modern era, Pep Guardiola, declared while Liverpool’s current boss, Iraola, was coaching on the south coast. “Today, modern football is not positional, you have to ride the rhythm, it is unbelievable.”

Iraola had the Cherries playing at concussive speeds both in and out of possession, an approach he has been building into Liverpool’s game during his four months on Merseyside. As Arteta warned ahead of his side’s trip to Anfield: “This is a team that is very vertical, they have the capacity to generate chaos from almost every situation.”

Arsenal, a side very much built on the principle of control rather than chaos, managed to corral their hosts for the opening quarter-hour, taking an entirely deserved 1–0 lead without letting Liverpool take a single shot or penetrate their box once. Yet, the Reds went into the locker rooms with the most touches in the opposition penalty area ever recorded in a Premier League first half against the Gunners (28).

Liverpool’s energy overwhelmed Arsenal, who were frantically clinging to a lead that looked remarkably slender. There was a sense of desperation about the way Arteta’s side dug in, defending like men lashed together on the deck of a ship in a full-blown storm. Yet, this was a battle Arsenal had anticipated.
“I expect big chaos in the game,” Gabriel predicted prematch, a glint of mischief in the center back’s eye. “We are ready.”

This is the challenge that Arteta has been building toward since he took over the club in 2019, steadily compiling a roster based upon grit as much as grace. The physical profile of the XI with which Arsenal ended the game was telling; eight were over six foot, a meaty wall of flesh almost welcoming the challenge of Liverpool’s attacking onslaught during those closing stages. “That togetherness we have is undefeated,” Declan Rice breathlessly gushed at the final whistle.
Yet, that Liverpool were even in a position to deliver such an onslaught should offer cause for optimism.

There will be a sense of what could have been for Andoni Iraola. / Darren Staples/AFP/Getty ImagesThe weight of history behind this fixture would suggest that the Reds would dominate, but, in truth, Arsenal should always have been considered favorites for this contest. The reigning champions finished 25 points above Liverpool last season while Arteta has more than six years of a head start on the recently appointed Iraola.

Faced with this tilted context, the Reds can take solace from the stack of chances that they created against the Gunners. Iraola’s side rattled off 17 shots by the end—no club has managed more when faced with this parsimonious Arsenal team since Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League final.

Much will be made of the fact that not a single effort was classified as ‘on target’—it’s remarkable to think that Dominik Szoboszlai’s free kick from August 2025 is the last shot Liverpool have directed at a goal defended by David Raya—but that is something of a misnomer. So many efforts were narrowly skewed wide from glorious positions as the hosts amassed an xG of 1.15. On most other days, they score.

Declan Rice has evolved this season. / Michael Steele/Getty ImagesArteta used to proudly call Rice Arsenal’s “lighthouse,” a towering figure who shone the beam on his teammates. He now needs a new nickname. “You are not the lighthouse anymore. You are something else,” Arteta told his midfielder at the end of last season. Now, the spotlight is perennially on Rice himself.

Everyone in Arsenal’s lineup has been given more positional freedom this season, but few more so than Rice. The former source of defensive ballast is now a two-way force of nature, as evidenced by his buccaneering, overlapping run around Noni Madueke’s right shoulder before sliding the ball across the box for the game’s opening goal. Rarely would Rice venture out of the left half of the pitch in years gone by, now he is wreaking havoc from the right byline.

This change of role has seen Rice’s creative output explode. The England international has racked up five Premier League assists already this term, all of which—intriguingly for a set-piece specialist—have come from open play.

Jurriën Timber got away with one. / Sky Sports.By the end of a blistering first half, Liverpool could be forgiven for wondering how they were not ahead, let alone trailing their visitors. Wayward finishing and some desperate blocks spared Arsenal but referee Andy Madley also played his part.

The official failed to spot a blatant tug of Alexander Isak’s shirt from Jurriën Timber, who had a full grubby mitt stretching the red fabric. There was oddly no great protestation from Liverpool’s No. 9, who exchanging a cheery look with Timber, but everyone else on Merseyside was furious.
